sections.title: Origins and banking in ancient India

blocks.text: Banking is about 2,000 years old. In Mesopotamia and Babylonia, lenders gave grain loans to farmers and to traders who carried goods between cities. Later, ancient Greece and the Roman Empire added two big innovations: **accepting deposits** and **changing money**.

blocks.title: Key terms
rows: A financial institution that accepts different forms of deposits, lends them to borrowers, and lets depositors withdraw their money from their accounts by **cheque**.
Lending money at an excessive rate of interest. The **Vedas** are the earliest Indian texts to mention it.
Loan-deed forms found in the Vedic literature. They recorded the names of debtor and creditor, loan amount, rate of interest, condition of repayment and time of repayment.
An instrument of the **Mauryan era**: an order to a banker to pay the sum on the note to a third person. It matches the idea of a modern **bill of exchange**.
The Italian name under which the idea of the modern banking system was conceptualised.

blocks.title: Early milestones in India
items: Debt, usury and loan deeds (rinapatra) are mentioned in the Vedas.
The **adesha**, a forerunner of the bill of exchange, is in use.
Loan deeds continue as dastawez; hundis and barattes appear (see the next sections).

blocks.title: Scriptures talk about money
blocks.text: Archaeological evidence suggests that banking practices and rules on debt were already referred to in India's scriptures and ancient texts, long before modern banks arrived.

**Indigenous bankers** lend money, act as money changers and finance India's internal trade through **hundis** (internal bills of exchange). This is one of the oldest banking systems and has worked for centuries. It started declining when the British came, yet it still holds a prominent place in the Indian money market today.

blocks.title: Defects of indigenous banking
items: It is **unorganised** and does not recognise the needs and working of the different sectors of the economy, including the banking sector.
It deals only with trade and commerce and works on a commission basis, which creates trade risk in their financial business.
It does not separate **short-term** and **long-term** finance.
Accounting follows local practice, so it cannot match modern financial accounting methods.
Many indigenous bankers charge a very high rate of interest.

blocks.title: Hundi vs adesha
blocks.text: A **hundi** is the credit instrument of indigenous banking (and it lasted into the Mughal period). The **adesha** belongs to the Mauryan era. Both behave like a bill of exchange, so do not mix up their eras.

Loan deeds carried on into the Mughal era under the name **dastawez**. Royal treasuries issued payment orders called **barattes**, and **hundis** (a type of credit instrument) evolved in this period and stayed in use.

blocks.title: Old Indian credit instruments in era order
blocks.phrase: Real Armies Deliver Big Hauls: Rinapatra, Adesha, Dastawez, Baratte, Hundi.
letters: Adesha: Mauryan order to pay (like a bill of exchange)
Dastawez: Mughal loan deed (e-talab = on demand, e-miadi = after time)
Baratte: payment orders of royal treasuries
Hundi: internal bill of exchange of indigenous bankers
blocks.note: Eras run Vedic, Mauryan, Mughal, so the first three letters R-A-D are also in time order.

sections.title: The first modern banks: Hindustan, Presidency and Imperial

blocks.text: The period from the coming of the Europeans (15th century) to Independence in 1947 laid the real foundation of modern banking in India. It saw a very large number of banks (more than 600). The first one was the **Bank of Hindustan**, set up in Calcutta (now Kolkata) in **1770** by M/s Alexander and Co. It ceased to operate in 1832.

The British East India Company had trading posts and factories in India and needed funds for its administrative, economic and military ambitions. So it set up three **Presidency Banks** under charters from the Company.

blocks.title: The three Presidency Banks
rows: 1st Presidency Bank, set up with the East India Company and the Government of Bengal. Total capital ₹50 lakh, of which ₹10 lakh came from the Company. Started as Bank of Calcutta and was renamed Bank of Bengal on 2 January 1809. In 1862, at Cawnpore, Dacca Bank (est. 1846) was amalgamated with it.
2nd Presidency Bank. It did all the normal activities expected of a commercial bank.
3rd Presidency Bank. Formed by amalgamating several existing regional banks and headquartered in Madras.

blocks.text: The **Imperial Bank of India** was formed on **27 January 1921** by amalgamating the Bank of Bengal, the Bank of Bombay and the Bank of Madras. It was a private entity till then. In **1955** it was nationalised and renamed **State Bank of India**, so SBI is the **oldest bank in India among the banks that exist today**.

blocks.title: Presidency Banks: order and years
blocks.phrase: Be Brave, Move! Bengal 1806, Bombay 1840, Madras 1843. From 1806 to 1840 is 34 years; then only 3 more.
blocks.note: The gaps 34 and 3 help you fix the years: 1806 + 34 = 1840, then 1840 + 3 = 1843.

blocks.title: Imperial Bank and SBI years
blocks.phrase: 19-21 three became one (Imperial); 19-55 the five-five: SBI Act 1955, and SBI later held 55% of its subsidiaries.
blocks.note: Imperial Bank: 1921. SBI: 1955. The number 55 shows up again in the 55:45 holding of subsidiary banks.

sections.title: Joint stock banks and other notable banks

blocks.text: A bank that has many shareholders is a **joint stock bank**. Limited liability was introduced in India in **1860**, which led to the setting up of joint stock banks. Indian joint stock banks were generally undercapitalised and lacked the experience and maturity to compete with the Presidency Banks.

blocks.title: Notable banks still operating
rows: Founded in Allahabad by a group of British. One of the oldest joint stock banks still working and one of the oldest public sector banks in India.
Established in Lahore (Punjab province) by Lala Lajpat Rai, Babu Purshotam Lal Tandon, S. Dayal Singh and others. The first bank purely managed by Indians.

Set up by Indian nationalists; the first Indian commercial bank wholly owned and managed by Indians, called the first truly **Swadeshi** bank. Founder: Sir Sorabji Pochkhanawala; first Chairman: Sir Pherozeshah Mehta.
Started as a private entity in 1906. It was the first Indian bank to open a foreign branch (London, 1946).

blocks.title: Notable banks that failed (now defunct)
rows: Set up by Indian merchants; failed within a decade.
The oldest joint stock bank of India; it failed in 1913.
Set up at Faizabad. It was the first bank in India with limited liability managed by an Indian board. It failed in 1958, after Independence.

blocks.title: Years of Indian joint stock banks
blocks.phrase: Allahabad alive at 65, Oudh old at 81, PNB at 94, Central eleven (1911). Upper India was 63 and failed in 13.

blocks.title: Many 'firsts', check the wording
blocks.text: Oudh Commercial Bank = first with limited liability and an Indian board (1881). PNB = first bank purely managed by Indians (1894). Central Bank = first wholly Indian-owned and managed commercial bank (1911). Bank of Upper India = oldest joint stock bank (1863, defunct).

sections.title: Birth of the Reserve Bank of India

blocks.text: In **1926** the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance, popularly the **Hilton-Young Commission**, submitted its report and recommended that the British Government of India create a **central bank**.

blocks.title: Objectives set out
items: To separate the control of **currency and credit** from the government.
To increase (augment) banking facilities throughout the country.

blocks.text: Finally, on **1 April 1935**, the Reserve Bank of India was established under the **RBI Act of 1934**, as the banker to the central government.

blocks.title: Hilton-Young to RBI
blocks.phrase: Twenty-six asks, thirty-four writes, thirty-five starts: 1926 report, 1934 Act, 1935 start.
letters: 1926: Hilton-Young Commission recommends a central bank

sections.title: After Independence: planning and the birth of SBI

blocks.text: After Independence, the RBI set up the **All India Rural Credit Survey Committee**. It recommended that the Imperial Bank of India be taken over and that the former state-owned and state-associated banks be merged or integrated with it.

India adopted planned economic development, aiming at social ownership of the means of production. Yet commercial banks were then private and were seen as controlled by business houses. They failed to meet the credit needs of poorer sections such as cottage and village industry, farmers and craftsmen. In **1950-51** there were **430** commercial banks.

blocks.title: The five subsidiary banks taken over in 1959 (as per the book)
items: State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur

blocks.text: In the subsidiary arrangement, **55%** of the capital was owned by SBI and **45%** stayed with the old shareholders. The model also showed weaknesses: lower bank profitability, a weak capital base and a heavy burden of **bad loans** (unrecovered loans).

blocks.title: Five SBI subsidiaries (old associates)
blocks.phrase: Put Hot Tea Before Me: Patiala, Hyderabad, Travancore, Bikaner and Jaipur, Mysore.
letters: State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur
blocks.note: These five and Bharatiya Mahila Bank merged into SBI on 1 April 2017.

blocks.title: Dates to fix
blocks.text: First Five Year Plan: 1951. SBI Act: 1955 (SBI formed on 1 July 1955 from the Imperial Bank). Subsidiary Banks Act: 1959. Bank count in 1950-51: 430.

blocks.title: Banking milestones after Independence
items: India implements its First Five Year Plan.
SBI constituted under the State Bank of India Act, 1955.
SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act passed; SBI takes over five former state-associate banks.
Deposit Insurance Corporation of India established (DIC Act 1961) to protect small depositors' deposits.
Agricultural Refinance Corporation (ARC) formed to refinance central land mortgage banks, state cooperative banks and scheduled commercial banks.
Cooperative banks brought under RBI regulation; the rupee is devalued for the first time.
National Credit Council (NCC) set up to help the Government and RBI reallocate credit according to plan priorities.
Lead Bank Scheme introduced to mobilise deposits on a massive scale and to step up lending to weaker sections.
Fourteen banks with deposits of over ₹50 crore are nationalised.
Differential Rate of Interest (DRI) scheme instituted for the weaker sections.
Priority Sector concept set up in Nov 1974 for public sector banks and in Nov 1978 for private sector banks.
Six banks with demand and time liabilities above ₹200 crore (as on 14.03.1980) nationalised.
Board for Financial Supervision (BFS) set up within RBI, exclusively for supervisory functions.
Banking Ombudsman Scheme introduced under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
BCSBI (Banking Codes and Standards Board of India) set up for voluntary registration of banks, committing to customer service as per agreed standards.

blocks.title: Nationalisation numbers
blocks.phrase: Sixty-nine = fourteen banks over ₹50 crore; Eighty = six banks over ₹200 crore. Total 14 + 6 = 20 banks; the limit rose 4 times.
letters: 6 banks (15 April); demand and time liabilities above ₹200 crore

blocks.title: Institutions of the 1960s and 70s in order
blocks.phrase: Deposits Are Never Lost, Dear People: DIC 1962, ARC 1963, NCC 1968, Lead Bank 1969, DRI 1972, Priority Sector 1974.

blocks.title: Do not confuse the 1969 events
blocks.text: Two different 1969 events: the **Lead Bank Scheme** (one bank for each district-type area, service area approach) and the **nationalisation of 14 banks**. Also, the Banking Ombudsman Scheme is 1995 while BCSBI is 2006.

In August 2019 the government announced the biggest consolidation of the banking space so far: **10 public sector banks merged into 4 bigger banks**, effective **1 April 2020**. Customers of the merging banks became customers of the banks they merged into. The number of public sector banks was to fall from **27 (in 2017) to 12**.

Mughal-era loan deeds were dastawez: e-indultalab (on demand) and e-miadi (after a fixed time); royal treasuries used barattes.

Oudh Commercial Bank (1881, Faizabad) was the first limited-liability bank with an Indian board; it failed in 1958.
Bank of India (private, 1906) opened the first foreign branch of an Indian bank (London, 1946).
